Protocol

GetClientConfigsSubscriptionRequest

The request has no specific fields in version 0: the client instance id arrives in the request header, selected through the headerVersions property that KIP-1313 adds to request schemas (header version 3 carries the client instance id).


GetClientConfigsSubscriptionResponse

Both RPCs are advertised only when client.configs.plugin.class is set on the broker.


PushClientConfigsRequest

Notes:

  • after a GetClientConfigsSubscription response that requests anything, the client sends the requested configs in one PushClientConfigsRequest, from its network thread and without blocking any user API call
  • the exchange runs once per client instance
  • the client retries only when no response arrives, using retry.backoff.ms within default.api.timeout.ms, and any response ends the exchange
  • Type is the ordinal of org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ConfigEntry.ConfigType. UNKNOWN means exactly one thing: the sending client does not define the key
    • such entries are not pushed in this version, and the broker drops any that arrive
    • a client library whose built-in type does not map onto ConfigEntry.ConfigType sends the key as STRING, never as UNKNOWN
  • Source tell where the config value comes from:
    • 0 for a default value
    • 1 for a value set by the application
    • 2 and above can be used future versions (e.g., 2 could be used for a broker-enforced value)
  • a Kafka Streams admin client sends two pushes of this RPC, one with ClientType=admin and one with ClientType=org.apache.kafka.streams (see Kafka Streams)


PushClientConfigsResponse

ErrorMessage carries a brief reason for an error (e.g., on CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE it states the broker's limit). This response does not wait for the plugin to run.

Errors

  • Both RPCs carry a top-level ErrorCode and ErrorMessage
  • Both RPCs can return UNSUPPORTED_VERSION if the feature is off on the broker (no plugin configured), or the requested version is not supported
  • PushClientConfigs can additionally return:
    • CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE:
      • indicates that the serialized snapshot exceeds the broker's client.configs.max.bytes
      • ErrorMessage states the limit
      • checked before the plugin is invoked
      • added by this KIP with its exception ClientConfigsTooLargeException, not retriable
    • INVALID_REQUEST:
      • malformed push (including a ClientType outside its format or length limit)
  • Client-side handling on any error:
    • log the broker's message once at WARN
    • end the exchange (no retry)
    • the client keeps operating normally and nothing reaches the application
    • only a missing response (timeout or disconnect) is retried, as described under Client Behavior
  • plugin outcomes are not reported to the client, so there is no plugin error code
  • throttling applies to both RPCs through ThrottleTimeMs and is not an error
  • pushing configurations is performed on a best-effort basis. Failure to send the configuration should not prevent the client from functioning.

Proposed Changes

Disabling the Feature

This feature can be disabled on the broker and the client.

For the broker, the feature is disabled by leaving the client.configs.plugin.class unset. The ApiVersions response then does not advertise the RPCs, and clients send nothing. With the plugin set but client.configs.requested.keys empty, clients ask once which keys are requested and nothing is collected. Given that this configuration is dynamic, this is a way of stopping collection without a broker roll.

For the client, set enable.config.push to false: the client does not send any of the 2 requests and behaves exactly like a client without the feature. 

Broker Behavior

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription and PushClientConfigs are included in ApiVersionsResponse only when client.configs.plugin.class is set
    • a request for either RPC while the feature is off gets a response with with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
  • no authorization performed by the broker on any of the 2 RPCs
    • any authenticated client may ask what is requested and report its own configuration
    • the plugin receives the principal and may apply its own authorization rule
  • When receiving a GetClientConfigsSubscription request the broker just returns the current value of the config client.configs.requested.keys. The plugin is not invoked.
  • When receiving a PushClientConfigs request the broker performs the following steps in this order:
    • validate push
      • the broker validated the push, checking the serialized size of the configs against client.configs.max.bytes (CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE) and well-formedness, including the ClientType rule (INVALID_REQUEST), before anything else.
    • filter configs against the requested set
      • entries not named in the current requested set, and entries typed UNKNOWN (keys the sending client does not define), are dropped before the plugin and logged at DEBUG by key name. This makes the operator's setting hold for every client library, and "built-in keys only" hold even for a client that does not filter. If nothing remains, the push is acknowledged without invoking the plugin.
    • invoke plugin (returns a future)
    • respond with ErrorCode=NONE without and waiting for the plugin's future
      • the future's outcome, including a synchronous throw, is recorded in the broker's metrics and logs and is not reported to the client
  • No storage or persisted state in the broker. Every accepted snapshot is handed to the plugin and then forgotten; a resend reaches the plugin again

Configuration Payload Size Enforcement

As described below, client implementations should not attempt to send a payload that is too large in the first place. But as a backup means of preventing the client from sending too much data, the broker checks the new configuration client.config.max.bytes prior to invoking the policy. If the size of the PushConfig request exceeds client.config.max.bytes, the broker returns the CONFIG_TOO_LARGE error to the client.

After analyzing the different Java clients’ configuration, a default of 10 KB for client.config.max.bytes provides more than sufficient capacity:

Excluding Sensitive Configuration

As explained in the concepts section, the ClientConfigPolicy implementation may also provide logic to ensure that clients do not send sensitive configuration. Clients across the Apache Kafka ecosystem do not have a consistent naming convention. As a result, brokers cannot determine sensitivity based on the configuration key name and rely on the incoming ConfigType field. When the ClientConfigPolicy detects sensitive configuration, it includes a description of the violation in the RPC response.

Client Behavior

Handshake

A client that supports this configuration interface will identify a node that supports the API using ApiVersions. The client performs a handshake by collecting the values for its configuration issuing a PushConfig RPC to submit the configuration to the broker node. The client sends the RPC after authentication (if any) and before the client starts to use the connection for requests. Similar to the ApiVersions handshake, the PushConfig RPC specifies a fixed timeout of default.timeout.ms. If the RPC exhausts its retries, the client logs the error, but continues execution.

Here’s the sequence:

  1. Client connects to broker

  2. Send ApiVersions request (internal, automatic)

  3. Receive ApiVersions response to determine which features broker supports

  4. If enable.config.push is set and configuration push is supported by the broker

    1. Collect requested client configuration values

    2. Send PushConfig with configuration

    3. Receive PushConfig response

  5. User requests can now be sent

The client chooses a randomly selected node for its configuration handshake, in the same way as GetTelemetrySubscriptions. The client configuration is only sent once, not for each broker. The “handshake” is performed on a per-client basis, not for each connection. As connections are closed due to disconnects or aging out, no new configuration handshake is performed. This operation is executed once for each distinct client instance.

The handshake is performed on a best-effort basis. Network or other transient errors that occur when transmitting the configuration data must not prevent the client from functioning.

Blocking Behavior

From the user’s perspective, the client blocks when a client API is invoked until the handshake completes.

For example:

producer = new KafkaProducer<>(props); // ✓ Non-blocking // First send() blocks until connection is ready (including configuration handshake) producer.send(record); // ← Blocks up to max.block.ms waiting for READY state]]>

Excluding Sensitive Configuration

The configuration entries sent in the PushConfig request should exclude any sensitive information. Which configuration keys are considered sensitive is determined by the client library.

Including Configuration Data Types

Depending on the server-side implementation, preserving the data types enables more compact storage, reduces redundant conversion, reduce cognitive overhead in downstream use, and eliminate invalid data (e.g. storing a value of “hi!” in a boolean). It’s also important because the server is not aware of all the different clients and their respective configuration, so providing the name, type, and value, though at times redundant, allows for wider client compatibility.

Metrics

This KIP does not introduce any new client metrics.

Rejected Alternatives

Exclusion of Default Values

The number of configuration entries is getting larger with each release, the vast majority of which use default settings. The question arises: how should we handle configuration entries that use a default value? Here are some options for the client:

  1. Send all configuration entries to the cluster, including those with default values.

  2. Omit any configuration entries that use their respective default values.

  3. Send all configuration entries, but omit the value value and demarcate those that use default values.

It’s redundant to send configuration with known default values. Preparing and sending the name, type, and value for scores of configuration could add up to a couple of KB in network transit. Additionally, that then means that the server side node that receives the handshake request then has to handle requests that consist mostly of entries with default values. It’s easy to argue that the defaults are superfluous and not include them.

Whether or not to include configuration entries with default values somewhat depends on what the ClientConfigPolicy implementation plans to do with those entries. Also, keep in mind that the server receiving the handshakes may service many different clients from different languages and versions. Even though the client knows when the configuration entry’s value is the default value, the broker handling the handshake may have no idea that, for example, topic.compression.level=low from the 2.5.2 version of the Visual Basic Kafka client is the default value for that client. Requiring each implementor of ClientConfigPolicy to maintain a listing of all the default values across all available Kafka clients and their respective versions seems like overkill.

The stance of this KIP is that there is no need to exclude default configuration, based on the following:

  1. The configuration handshake only occurs once during the lifetime of a client.

  2. The configuration handshake request size is negligible compared with the amount of network traffic over the course of the lifetime of a client.

  3. The server node handling the incoming configuration handshake can drop any entries that come in with a default value.

Requiring that broker know a priori the default values (to fill in the missing information) is a maintenance problem.

Including Configuration Storage Detail

Storage and retention of the configuration data is outside the scope of this KIP. The ClientConfigPolicy implementation is responsible for managing the storage, if any, of the configuration payload once the broker invokes it.

Motivation

Client configuration represents the number one pain point hindering organizations' adoption and expansion of Kafka. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. Additionally, the teams developing and deploying client applications in an organization are often separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the organization's Kafka cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). This complexity unnecessarily delays projects and contributes to operational overhead, as configuration tuning often requires specialized expertise.

As Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical. This KIP takes the first step in solving this issue by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Clients push the requested keys once, at startup, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows. 

At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance and framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. And most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps: each client instance pushes one snapshot of the requested keys, carrying the identifiers needed to group it (client instance id, client id, client type and the framework identifiers, piggybacking on KIP-1313 and KIP-1368), and the receiving broker hands it to an operator-supplied plugin.

This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework pushes one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does in this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.

The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is then collected is a reviewed default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name, before or after enabling.

It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications. 

This KIP delivers observability only. Its building blocks (two RPCs and a plugin interface) are shaped so that follow-up KIPs can add extend upon it (e.g., support enforcement)

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds a new RPC to the Kafka protocol that forms a handshake between the client and broker, named PushConfig, by which the client sends the configuration (keys and values) to the broker. Brokers interact with a new ClientConfigPolicy interface to process the RPC from the client.

This KIP adds two new RPCs (in the same shape as KIP-714 for telemetry):

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription : used by clients to asks the cluster which configuration keys it requests
  • PushClientConfigs : used to send those keys once, at startup, without blocking its own operation

Brokers hand the configuration to a new ClientConfigsPlugin  interface.

The KIP also adds broker and client configurations, and one public client method for frameworks such as Kafka Streams.

Definitions

Client Instance ID

KIP-714 introduced it as a UUID that identifies one client instance for telemetry, and KIP-1313 makes it available for all paths: the client generates it at construction and sends it in request header version 3 on the first request of every connection, and the broker caches it for that connection. 

This KIP builds on top of KIP-1313: both new RPCs use request header version 3, which carries the client instance id.

The configuration exchange is independent of KIP-714 telemetry: a client may use one, the other or both, and they may go to different brokers. The plugins access the client instance id universally provided by KIP-1313. See detail of accessors below.

Configurations sent

A key is pushed when the cluster asks for it and the client is willing to send it. The cluster asks through the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys . The client decides whether to send the config or not based on three tiers:

TierDefinitionSent when
0. Never pushed
  • any key of type PASSWORD in Kafka's existing ConfigDef.Type
  • any key in the sasl., ssl. or security. families (as a prefix, or an infix such as producer.ssl.)
  • bootstrap.servers and bootstrap.controllers
  • never, even if requested
    • the client filters them out (no overrides)
    • exclusion hard-coded in every client implementation
1. Built-in
  • every other key defined in the client's own configuration definition (ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig, AdminClientConfig, StreamsConfig, ShareConsumerConfig), including Type.CLASS keys
  • the key is named in the requested set AND
  • not matched by config.push.denied.keys.
2. Custom
  • any key present in the client's configuration but not defined by the client (e.g., serializer/interceptor/partitioner/application settings, config.providers.*, and any other keys the application may add)
  • never in this KIP, even if named in the requested set
    • see Future Work for potential follow-ups


Other considerations:

  • requested keys the client does not define are ignored by the client
    • if a client sends one anyway, the broker drops it before invoking the plugin (see Broker Behavior).
  • requested keys are pushed whether or not they hold the default value, and a "Source" field added by this KIP to each entry (indicating if the value is default or user-defined).
  • tier 0 (never pushed) is filtered on the key, before any value is rendered, with the deny list supporting prefixes to easily reduce what is sent (e.g., any key in the form of sasl., ssl. or security.)
  • if nothing remains after filtering, the client sends nothing.
  • on every push the client logs at INFO the keys it pushed and the requested keys it filtered out, with the reason (tier 0, denied, not defined), never the values. With this an application can audit from its own log what left the process
  • custom keys are deferred. Keys the client does not define are the one category whose sensitivity Kafka cannot judge, and no requirement needs them yet. They are never pushed in this version, whatever the requested set says. The shape a later version would use, in which the application names the keys it is willing to share and the cluster opens the category, is recorded under Future Work.
  • class-name keys (key.serializer, value.deserializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes, partition.assignment.strategy, metric.reporters and similar) are tier 1:
    • when requested, the client pushes the fully qualified class names it is configured with, whether set by name or passed to the constructor;
    • they reveal the application's package naming and its choice of serializers, interceptors or partitioners, not credentials, endpoints or data, and they are among the most common root causes in client support cases;
    • none is in the default set, so they flow only when an operator requests them;
    • an application that prefers not to send them lists them in config.push.denied.keys, and an operator's plugin can drop them as well. Treating them as custom keys instead is listed under Rejected Alternatives.
    • Key names and tiers are the client library's own. The default requested set uses the Java client's names; a library whose names differ ignores names it does not define, and a library with a different naming convention adjusts its tier 0 rules accordingly
  • a few keys describe the environment rather than behavior: client.rack and, in Kafka Streams, application.server and state.dir. They are not sensitive configs filtered out by default, so an operator can request them by name; they are not in the default requested set, and an application that prefers not to send them can exclude them by adding them to config.push.denied.keys.

Default Configuration for Apache Kafka clients

The default value for the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys  is one list for all client types. It includes:

  • identity keys that let a plugin group snapshots by application, consumer group, transactional producer or Streams application (client.id, group.id, group.instance.id, transactional.id, application.id)

  • the list contains no class names and no custom keys
  • each client sends the requested keys it supports and ignores the rest

Client Configuration Plugins

This KIP introduces a new broker-side interface named ClientConfigsPlugin.

  • invoked asynchronously with each accepted configuration snapshot
  • it does not validate the configuration
  • each implementation can take any desired action on the received config snapshot: log, forward it, store it, etc.
  • operators install an implementation through the broker configuration described later
  • no implementation shipped with Kafka
  • its shape follows the asynchronous plugin interface introduced by KIP-1331

The flow includes the following steps:

  2. If client.configs.plugin.class  is configured, the broker advertises GetClientConfigsSubscription  and PushClientConfigs  in the ApiVersions response

About rolls and restarts

  • enabling the feature is one broker roll (to set the plugin class) and no client restart. Every running client reconnects during the roll, sees the RPCs advertised for the first time, and runs its exchange.
  • a later change to the requested set is one command and no roll, but it reaches running clients only at their next restart (clients runs its exchange once at startup). Operators should adjust the list before enabling the plugin.

Protocol

GetClientConfigsSubscriptionRequest

The request has no specific fields in version 0: the client instance id arrives in the request header, selected through the headerVersions property that KIP-1313 adds to request schemas (header version 3 carries the client instance id).


GetClientConfigsSubscriptionResponse

Both RPCs are advertised only when client.configs.plugin.class is set on the broker.


PushClientConfigsRequest

Notes:

  • after a GetClientConfigsSubscription response that requests anything, the client sends the requested configs in one PushClientConfigsRequest, from its network thread and without blocking any user API call
  • the exchange runs once per client instance
  • the client retries only when no response arrives, using retry.backoff.ms within default.api.timeout.ms, and any response ends the exchange
  • Type is the ordinal of org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ConfigEntry.ConfigType. UNKNOWN means exactly one thing: the sending client does not define the key
    • such entries are not pushed in this version, and the broker drops any that arrive
    • a client library whose built-in type does not map onto ConfigEntry.ConfigType sends the key as STRING, never as UNKNOWN
  • Source tell where the config value comes from:
    • 0 for a default value
    • 1 for a value set by the application
    • 2 and above can be used future versions (e.g., 2 could be used for a broker-enforced value)
  • a Kafka Streams admin client sends two pushes of this RPC, one with ClientType=admin and one with ClientType=org.apache.kafka.streams (see Kafka Streams)


PushClientConfigsResponse

ErrorMessage carries a brief reason for an error (e.g., on CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE it states the broker's limit). This response does not wait for the plugin to run.

Errors

  • Both RPCs carry a top-level ErrorCode and ErrorMessage
  • Both RPCs can return UNSUPPORTED_VERSION if the feature is off on the broker (no plugin configured), or the requested version is not supported
  • PushClientConfigs can additionally return:
    • CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE:
      • indicates that the serialized snapshot exceeds the broker's client.configs.max.bytes
      • ErrorMessage states the limit
      • checked before the plugin is invoked
      • added by this KIP with its exception ClientConfigsTooLargeException, not retriable
    • INVALID_REQUEST:
      • malformed push (including a ClientType outside its format or length limit)
  • Client-side handling on any error:
    • log the broker's message once at WARN
    • end the exchange (no retry)
    • the client keeps operating normally and nothing reaches the application
    • only a missing response (timeout or disconnect) is retried, as described under Client Behavior
  • plugin outcomes are not reported to the client, so there is no plugin error code
  • throttling applies to both RPCs through ThrottleTimeMs and is not an error
  • pushing configurations is performed on a best-effort basis. Failure to send the configuration should not prevent the client from functioning.

Proposed Changes

Disabling the Feature

This feature can be disabled on the broker and the client.

For the broker, the feature is disabled by leaving the client.configs.plugin.class unset. The ApiVersions response then does not advertise the RPCs, and clients send nothing. With the plugin set but client.configs.requested.keys empty, clients ask once which keys are requested and nothing is collected. Given that this configuration is dynamic, this is a way of stopping collection without a broker roll.

For the client, set enable.config.push to false: the client does not send any of the 2 requests and behaves exactly like a client without the feature. 

Broker Behavior

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription and PushClientConfigs are included in ApiVersionsResponse only when client.configs.plugin.class is set
    • a request for either RPC while the feature is off gets a response with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
  • no authorization performed by the broker on any of the 2 RPCs
    • any authenticated client may ask what is requested and report its own configuration
    • the plugin receives the principal and may apply its own authorization rule
  • when receiving a GetClientConfigsSubscription request the broker just returns the current value of the config client.configs.requested.keys.The plugin is not invoked.
  • when receiving a PushClientConfigs request the broker performs the following steps in this order:
    • validate push
      • the broker validates the push, checking the serialized size of the configs against client.configs.max.bytes (CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE) and well-formedness, including the ClientType rule (INVALID_REQUEST), before anything else.
    • filter configs against the requested set
      • entries not named in the current requested set, and entries typed UNKNOWN (keys the sending client does not define), are dropped before the plugin and logged at DEBUG by key name. This makes the operator's setting hold for every client library, and "built-in keys only" hold even for a client that does not filter. If nothing remains, the push is acknowledged without invoking the plugin.
    • invoke plugin (returns a future)
    • respond with ErrorCode=NONE without waiting for the plugin's future
      • the future's outcome, including a synchronous throw, is recorded in the broker's metrics and logs and is not reported to the client
  • no storage or persisted state in the broker. Every accepted snapshot is handed to the plugin and then forgotten; a resend reaches the plugin again
    • with this, the broker cannot tell apart a client that is older than this KIP or has enable.config.push=false (sends neither request), a client that had nothing left after filtering (sends no push), a client whose push was rejected as too large, and a client that gave up after no response. Every request header carries the client instance id (KIP-1313), so a system that records instance ids can still list the instances that never pushed.

Configuration Payload Size Enforcement

Clients only send the requested keys that belong to them, so a snapshot is small. As a backup, the broker checks the serialized size of every PushClientConfigs request against client.configs.max.bytes before invoking the plugin. If the request is larger, the broker answers CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE, with the limit in the error message, and nothing reaches the plugin.

A client's share of the default requested set is a few hundred bytes. The limit only matters if an operator requests every key a client defines. The table shows that worst case for the Java clients, so a default of 10 KB leaves room:

Excluding sensitive configurations

  • sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered (hardcoded sensitive set)
  • the broker does not check sensitivity
  • the broker only drops entries that are not in the requested set and entries typed UNKNOWN (see above)
  • a plugin may drop more (for example class-name keys); the client is not told about it

Client Behavior

Handshake

A client that supports this configuration interface will identify a node that supports the API using ApiVersions. The client performs a handshake by collecting the values for its configuration issuing a PushConfig RPC to submit the configuration to the broker node. The client sends the RPC after authentication (if any) and before the client starts to use the connection for requests. Similar to the ApiVersions handshake, the PushConfig RPC specifies a fixed timeout of default.timeout.ms. If the RPC exhausts its retries, the client logs the error, but continues execution.

Here’s the sequence:

  1. Client connects to broker

  2. Send ApiVersions request (internal, automatic)

  3. Receive ApiVersions response to determine which features broker supports

  4. If enable.config.push is set and configuration push is supported by the broker

    1. Collect requested client configuration values

    2. Send PushConfig with configuration

    3. Receive PushConfig response

  5. User requests can now be sent

The client chooses a randomly selected node for its configuration handshake, in the same way as GetTelemetrySubscriptions. The client configuration is only sent once, not for each broker. The “handshake” is performed on a per-client basis, not for each connection. As connections are closed due to disconnects or aging out, no new configuration handshake is performed. This operation is executed once for each distinct client instance.

The handshake is performed on a best-effort basis. Network or other transient errors that occur when transmitting the configuration data must not prevent the client from functioning.

Blocking Behavior

From the user’s perspective, the client blocks when a client API is invoked until the handshake completes.

For example:

producer = new KafkaProducer<>(props); // ✓ Non-blocking // First send() blocks until connection is ready (including configuration handshake) producer.send(record); // ← Blocks up to max.block.ms waiting for READY state]]>

Excluding Sensitive Configuration

The configuration entries sent in the PushConfig request should exclude any sensitive information. Which configuration keys are considered sensitive is determined by the client library.

Including Configuration Data Types

Depending on the server-side implementation, preserving the data types enables more compact storage, reduces redundant conversion, reduce cognitive overhead in downstream use, and eliminate invalid data (e.g. storing a value of “hi!” in a boolean). It’s also important because the server is not aware of all the different clients and their respective configuration, so providing the name, type, and value, though at times redundant, allows for wider client compatibility.

Metrics

This KIP does not introduce any new client metrics.

Rejected Alternatives

Exclusion of Default Values

The number of configuration entries is getting larger with each release, the vast majority of which use default settings. The question arises: how should we handle configuration entries that use a default value? Here are some options for the client:

  1. Send all configuration entries to the cluster, including those with default values.

  2. Omit any configuration entries that use their respective default values.

  3. Send all configuration entries, but omit the value value and demarcate those that use default values.

It’s redundant to send configuration with known default values. Preparing and sending the name, type, and value for scores of configuration could add up to a couple of KB in network transit. Additionally, that then means that the server side node that receives the handshake request then has to handle requests that consist mostly of entries with default values. It’s easy to argue that the defaults are superfluous and not include them.

Whether or not to include configuration entries with default values somewhat depends on what the ClientConfigPolicy implementation plans to do with those entries. Also, keep in mind that the server receiving the handshakes may service many different clients from different languages and versions. Even though the client knows when the configuration entry’s value is the default value, the broker handling the handshake may have no idea that, for example, topic.compression.level=low from the 2.5.2 version of the Visual Basic Kafka client is the default value for that client. Requiring each implementor of ClientConfigPolicy to maintain a listing of all the default values across all available Kafka clients and their respective versions seems like overkill.

The stance of this KIP is that there is no need to exclude default configuration, based on the following:

  1. The configuration handshake only occurs once during the lifetime of a client.

  2. The configuration handshake request size is negligible compared with the amount of network traffic over the course of the lifetime of a client.

  3. The server node handling the incoming configuration handshake can drop any entries that come in with a default value.

Requiring that broker know a priori the default values (to fill in the missing information) is a maintenance problem.

Including Configuration Storage Detail

Storage and retention of the configuration data is outside the scope of this KIP. The ClientConfigPolicy implementation is responsible for managing the storage, if any, of the configuration payload once the broker invokes it.

Motivation

Client configuration represents the number one pain point hindering organizations' adoption and expansion of Kafka. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. Additionally, the teams developing and deploying client applications in an organization are often separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the organization's Kafka cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). This complexity unnecessarily delays projects and contributes to operational overhead, as configuration tuning often requires specialized expertise.

As Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical. This KIP takes the first step in solving this issue by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Clients push the requested keys once, at startup, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows. 

At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance and framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. And most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps: each client instance pushes one snapshot of the requested keys, carrying the identifiers needed to group it (client instance id, client id, client type and the framework identifiers, piggybacking on KIP-1313 and KIP-1368), and the receiving broker hands it to an operator-supplied plugin.

This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework pushes one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does in this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.

The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is then collected is a reviewed default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name, before or after enabling.

It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications. 

This KIP delivers observability only. Its building blocks (two RPCs and a plugin interface) are shaped so that follow-up KIPs can add extend upon it (e.g., support enforcement)

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds a new RPC to the Kafka protocol that forms a handshake between the client and broker, named PushConfig, by which the client sends the configuration (keys and values) to the broker. Brokers interact with a new ClientConfigPolicy interface to process the RPC from the client.

This KIP adds two new RPCs (in the same shape as KIP-714 for telemetry):

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription : used by clients to asks the cluster which configuration keys it requests
  • PushClientConfigs : used to send those keys once, at startup, without blocking its own operation

Brokers hand the configuration to a new ClientConfigsPlugin  interface.

The KIP also adds broker and client configurations, and one public client method for frameworks such as Kafka Streams.

Definitions

Client Instance ID

KIP-714 introduced it as a UUID that identifies one client instance for telemetry, and KIP-1313 makes it available for all paths: the client generates it at construction and sends it in request header version 3 on the first request of every connection, and the broker caches it for that connection. 

This KIP builds on top of KIP-1313: both new RPCs use request header version 3, which carries the client instance id.

The configuration exchange is independent of KIP-714 telemetry: a client may use one, the other or both, and they may go to different brokers. The plugins access the client instance id universally provided by KIP-1313. See detail of accessors below.

Configurations sent

A key is pushed when the cluster asks for it and the client is willing to send it. The cluster asks through the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys . The client decides whether to send the config or not based on three tiers:

TierDefinitionSent when
0. Never pushed
  • any key of type PASSWORD in Kafka's existing ConfigDef.Type
  • any key in the sasl., ssl. or security. families (as a prefix, or an infix such as producer.ssl.)
  • bootstrap.servers and bootstrap.controllers
  • never, even if requested
    • the client filters them out (no overrides)
    • exclusion hard-coded in every client implementation
1. Built-in
  • every other key defined in the client's own configuration definition (ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig, AdminClientConfig, StreamsConfig, ShareConsumerConfig), including Type.CLASS keys
  • the key is named in the requested set AND
  • not matched by config.push.denied.keys.
2. Custom
  • any key present in the client's configuration but not defined by the client (e.g., serializer/interceptor/partitioner/application settings, config.providers.*, and any other keys the application may add)
  • never in this KIP, even if named in the requested set
    • see Future Work for potential follow-ups


Other considerations:

  • requested keys the client does not define are ignored by the client
    • if a client sends one anyway, the broker drops it before invoking the plugin (see Broker Behavior).
  • requested keys are pushed whether or not they hold the default value, and a "Source" field added by this KIP to each entry (indicating if the value is default or user-defined).
  • tier 0 (never pushed) is filtered on the key, before any value is rendered, with the deny list supporting prefixes to easily reduce what is sent (e.g., any key in the form of sasl., ssl. or security.)
  • if nothing remains after filtering, the client sends nothing.
  • on every push the client logs at INFO the keys it pushed and the requested keys it filtered out, with the reason (tier 0, denied, not defined), never the values. With this an application can audit from its own log what left the process
  • custom keys are deferred. Keys the client does not define are the one category whose sensitivity Kafka cannot judge, and no requirement needs them yet. They are never pushed in this version, whatever the requested set says. The shape a later version would use, in which the application names the keys it is willing to share and the cluster opens the category, is recorded under Future Work.
  • class-name keys (key.serializer, value.deserializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes, partition.assignment.strategy, metric.reporters and similar) are tier 1:
    • when requested, the client pushes the fully qualified class names it is configured with, whether set by name or passed to the constructor;
    • they reveal the application's package naming and its choice of serializers, interceptors or partitioners, not credentials, endpoints or data, and they are among the most common root causes in client support cases;
    • none is in the default set, so they flow only when an operator requests them;
    • an application that prefers not to send them lists them in config.push.denied.keys, and an operator's plugin can drop them as well. Treating them as custom keys instead is listed under Rejected Alternatives.
    • Key names and tiers are the client library's own. The default requested set uses the Java client's names; a library whose names differ ignores names it does not define, and a library with a different naming convention adjusts its tier 0 rules accordingly
  • a few keys describe the environment rather than behavior: client.rack and, in Kafka Streams, application.server and state.dir. They are not sensitive configs filtered out by default, so an operator can request them by name; they are not in the default requested set, and an application that prefers not to send them can exclude them by adding them to config.push.denied.keys.

The default value for the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys  is one list for all client types. It includes:

  • identity keys that let a plugin group snapshots by application, consumer group, transactional producer or Streams application (client.id, group.id, group.instance.id, transactional.id, application.id)

  • the list contains no class names and no custom keys
  • each client sends the requested keys it supports and ignores the rest

Client Configuration Plugins

This KIP introduces a new broker-side interface named ClientConfigsPlugin.

  • invoked asynchronously with each accepted configuration snapshot
  • it does not validate the configuration
  • each implementation can take any desired action on the received config snapshot: log, forward it, store it, etc.
  • operators install an implementation through the broker configuration described later
  • no implementation shipped with Kafka
  • its shape follows the asynchronous plugin interface introduced by KIP-1331

End-to-end Flow [OUTDATED - WIP]

The following sequence diagram shows the flow between the various entities:

The flow includes the following steps:

  1. The client establishes a connection to the broker and sends an ApiVersions request
  2. If client.configs.plugin.class  is configured, the broker advertises GetClientConfigsSubscription  and PushClientConfigs  in the ApiVersions response

  8. The client marks its exchange as complete for its lifetime. None of these steps blocks a user API call

About rolls and restarts

  • enabling the feature is one broker roll (to set the plugin class) and no client restart. Every running client reconnects during the roll, sees the RPCs advertised for the first time, and runs its exchange.
  • a later change to the requested set is one command and no roll, but it reaches running clients only at their next restart (clients runs its exchange once at startup). Operators should adjust the list before enabling the plugin.

Protocol

GetClientConfigsSubscriptionRequest

The request has no specific fields in version 0: the client instance id arrives in the request header, selected through the headerVersions property that KIP-1313 adds to request schemas (header version 3 carries the client instance id).


GetClientConfigsSubscriptionResponse

Both RPCs are advertised only when client.configs.plugin.class is set on the broker.


PushClientConfigsRequest

Notes:

  • after a GetClientConfigsSubscription response that requests anything, the client sends the requested configs in one PushClientConfigsRequest, from its network thread and without blocking any user API call
  • the exchange runs once per client instance
  • the client retries only when no response arrives, using retry.backoff.ms within default.api.timeout.ms, and any response ends the exchange
  • Type is the ordinal of org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ConfigEntry.ConfigType. UNKNOWN means exactly one thing: the sending client does not define the key
    • such entries are not pushed in this version, and the broker drops any that arrive
    • a client library whose built-in type does not map onto ConfigEntry.ConfigType sends the key as STRING, never as UNKNOWN
  • Source tell where the config value comes from:
    • 0 for a default value
    • 1 for a value set by the application
    • 2 and above can be used future versions (e.g., 2 could be used for a broker-enforced value)
  • a Kafka Streams admin client sends two pushes of this RPC, one with ClientType=admin and one with ClientType=org.apache.kafka.streams (see Kafka Streams)


PushClientConfigsResponse

ErrorMessage carries a brief reason for an error (e.g., on CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE it states the broker's limit). This response does not wait for the plugin to run.

Errors

  • Both RPCs carry a top-level ErrorCode and ErrorMessage
  • Both RPCs can return UNSUPPORTED_VERSION if the feature is off on the broker (no plugin configured), or the requested version is not supported
  • PushClientConfigs can additionally return:
    • CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE:
      • indicates that the serialized snapshot exceeds the broker's client.configs.max.bytes
      • ErrorMessage states the limit
      • checked before the plugin is invoked
      • added by this KIP with its exception ClientConfigsTooLargeException, not retriable
    • INVALID_REQUEST:
      • malformed push (including a ClientType outside its format or length limit)
  • Client-side handling on any error:
    • log the broker's message once at WARN
    • end the exchange (no retry)
    • the client keeps operating normally and nothing reaches the application
    • only a missing response (timeout or disconnect) is retried, as described under Client Behavior
  • plugin outcomes are not reported to the client, so there is no plugin error code
  • throttling applies to both RPCs through ThrottleTimeMs and is not an error
  • pushing configurations is performed on a best-effort basis. Failure to send the configuration should not prevent the client from functioning.

Proposed Changes

Disabling the Feature

This feature can be disabled on the broker and the client.

For the broker, the feature is disabled by leaving the client.configs.plugin.class unset. The ApiVersions response then does not advertise the RPCs, and clients send nothing. With the plugin set but client.configs.requested.keys empty, clients ask once which keys are requested and nothing is collected. Given that this configuration is dynamic, this is a way of stopping collection without a broker roll.

For the client, set enable.config.push to false: the client does not send any of the 2 requests and behaves exactly like a client without the feature. 

Broker Behavior

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription and PushClientConfigs are included in ApiVersionsResponse only when client.configs.plugin.class is set
    • a request for either RPC while the feature is off gets a response with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
  • no authorization performed by the broker on any of the 2 RPCs
    • any authenticated client may ask what is requested and report its own configuration
    • the plugin receives the principal and may apply its own authorization rule
  • when receiving a GetClientConfigsSubscription request the broker just returns the current value of the config client.configs.requested.keys.The plugin is not invoked.
  • when receiving a PushClientConfigs request the broker performs the following steps in this order:
    • validate push
      • the broker validates the push, checking the serialized size of the configs against client.configs.max.bytes (CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE) and well-formedness, including the ClientType rule (INVALID_REQUEST), before anything else.
    • filter configs against the requested set
      • entries not named in the current requested set, and entries typed UNKNOWN (keys the sending client does not define), are dropped before the plugin and logged at DEBUG by key name. This makes the operator's setting hold for every client library, and "built-in keys only" hold even for a client that does not filter. If nothing remains, the push is acknowledged without invoking the plugin.
    • invoke plugin (returns a future)
    • respond with ErrorCode=NONE without waiting for the plugin's future
      • the future's outcome, including a synchronous throw, is recorded in the broker's metrics and logs and is not reported to the client
  • no storage or persisted state in the broker. Every accepted snapshot is handed to the plugin and then forgotten; a resend reaches the plugin again
    • with this, the broker cannot tell apart a client that is older than this KIP or has enable.config.push=false (sends neither request), a client that had nothing left after filtering (sends no push), a client whose push was rejected as too large, and a client that gave up after no response. Every request header carries the client instance id (KIP-1313), so a system that records instance ids can still list the instances that never pushed.

Configuration payload size enforcement

Clients only send the requested keys that belong to them, so a snapshot is small. As a backup, the broker checks the serialized size of every PushClientConfigs request against client.configs.max.bytes before invoking the plugin. If the request is larger, the broker answers CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE, with the limit in the error message, and nothing reaches the plugin.

A client's share of the default requested set is a few hundred bytes. The limit only matters if an operator requests every key a client defines. The table shows that worst case for the Java clients, so a default of 10 KB leaves room:

A default 10 KB limit provides 2x headroom for a Kafka Streams snapshot with every key requested, and more than 10x for the default requested set, while preventing abuse from malicious clients.

Excluding sensitive configurations

  • sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered (hardcoded sensitive set)
  • the broker does not check sensitivity
  • the broker only drops entries that are not in the requested set and entries typed UNKNOWN (see above)
  • a plugin may drop more (for example class-name keys); the client is not told about it

Client Behavior

Handshake

A client that supports this configuration interface will identify a node that supports the API using ApiVersions. The client performs a handshake by collecting the values for its configuration issuing a PushConfig RPC to submit the configuration to the broker node. The client sends the RPC after authentication (if any) and before the client starts to use the connection for requests. Similar to the ApiVersions handshake, the PushConfig RPC specifies a fixed timeout of default.timeout.ms. If the RPC exhausts its retries, the client logs the error, but continues execution.

Here’s the sequence:

  1. Client connects to broker

  2. Send ApiVersions request (internal, automatic)

  3. Receive ApiVersions response to determine which features broker supports

  4. If enable.config.push is set and configuration push is supported by the broker

    1. Collect requested client configuration values

    2. Send PushConfig with configuration

    3. Receive PushConfig response

  5. User requests can now be sent

The client chooses a randomly selected node for its configuration handshake, in the same way as GetTelemetrySubscriptions. The client configuration is only sent once, not for each broker. The “handshake” is performed on a per-client basis, not for each connection. As connections are closed due to disconnects or aging out, no new configuration handshake is performed. This operation is executed once for each distinct client instance.

The handshake is performed on a best-effort basis. Network or other transient errors that occur when transmitting the configuration data must not prevent the client from functioning.

Blocking Behavior

From the user’s perspective, the client blocks when a client API is invoked until the handshake completes.

For example:

producer = new KafkaProducer<>(props); // ✓ Non-blocking // First send() blocks until connection is ready (including configuration handshake) producer.send(record); // ← Blocks up to max.block.ms waiting for READY state]]>

Excluding Sensitive Configuration

The configuration entries sent in the PushConfig request should exclude any sensitive information. Which configuration keys are considered sensitive is determined by the client library.

Including Configuration Data Types

Depending on the server-side implementation, preserving the data types enables more compact storage, reduces redundant conversion, reduce cognitive overhead in downstream use, and eliminate invalid data (e.g. storing a value of “hi!” in a boolean). It’s also important because the server is not aware of all the different clients and their respective configuration, so providing the name, type, and value, though at times redundant, allows for wider client compatibility.

Metrics

This KIP does not introduce any new client metrics.

Rejected Alternatives

Exclusion of Default Values

The number of configuration entries is getting larger with each release, the vast majority of which use default settings. The question arises: how should we handle configuration entries that use a default value? Here are some options for the client:

  1. Send all configuration entries to the cluster, including those with default values.

  2. Omit any configuration entries that use their respective default values.

  3. Send all configuration entries, but omit the value value and demarcate those that use default values.

It’s redundant to send configuration with known default values. Preparing and sending the name, type, and value for scores of configuration could add up to a couple of KB in network transit. Additionally, that then means that the server side node that receives the handshake request then has to handle requests that consist mostly of entries with default values. It’s easy to argue that the defaults are superfluous and not include them.

Whether or not to include configuration entries with default values somewhat depends on what the ClientConfigPolicy implementation plans to do with those entries. Also, keep in mind that the server receiving the handshakes may service many different clients from different languages and versions. Even though the client knows when the configuration entry’s value is the default value, the broker handling the handshake may have no idea that, for example, topic.compression.level=low from the 2.5.2 version of the Visual Basic Kafka client is the default value for that client. Requiring each implementor of ClientConfigPolicy to maintain a listing of all the default values across all available Kafka clients and their respective versions seems like overkill.

The stance of this KIP is that there is no need to exclude default configuration, based on the following:

  1. The configuration handshake only occurs once during the lifetime of a client.

  2. The configuration handshake request size is negligible compared with the amount of network traffic over the course of the lifetime of a client.

  3. The server node handling the incoming configuration handshake can drop any entries that come in with a default value.

Requiring that broker know a priori the default values (to fill in the missing information) is a maintenance problem.

Including Configuration Storage Detail

Storage and retention of the configuration data is outside the scope of this KIP. The ClientConfigPolicy implementation is responsible for managing the storage, if any, of the configuration payload once the broker invokes it.

Motivation

Client configuration represents the number one pain point hindering organizations' adoption and expansion of Kafka. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. Additionally, the teams developing and deploying client applications in an organization are often separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the organization's Kafka cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). This complexity unnecessarily delays projects and contributes to operational overhead, as configuration tuning often requires specialized expertise.

As Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical. This KIP takes the first step in solving this issue by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Clients push the requested keys once, at startup, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows. 

At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance and framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. And most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps: each client instance pushes one snapshot of the requested keys, carrying the identifiers needed to group it (client instance id, client id, client type and the framework identifiers, piggybacking on KIP-1313 and KIP-1368), and the receiving broker hands it to an operator-supplied plugin.

This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework pushes one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does in this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.

The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is then collected is a reviewed default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name, before or after enabling.

It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications. 

This KIP delivers observability only. Its building blocks (two RPCs and a plugin interface) are shaped so that follow-up KIPs can add extend upon it (e.g., support enforcement)

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds a new RPC to the Kafka protocol that forms a handshake between the client and broker, named PushConfig, by which the client sends the configuration (keys and values) to the broker. Brokers interact with a new ClientConfigPolicy interface to process the RPC from the client.

This KIP adds two new RPCs (in the same shape as KIP-714 for telemetry):

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription : used by clients to asks the cluster which configuration keys it requests
  • PushClientConfigs : used to send those keys once, at startup, without blocking its own operation

Brokers hand the configuration to a new ClientConfigsPlugin  interface.

The KIP also adds broker and client configurations, and one public client method for frameworks such as Kafka Streams.

Definitions

Client Instance ID

KIP-714 introduced it as a UUID that identifies one client instance for telemetry, and KIP-1313 makes it available for all paths: the client generates it at construction and sends it in request header version 3 on the first request of every connection, and the broker caches it for that connection. 

This KIP builds on top of KIP-1313: both new RPCs use request header version 3, which carries the client instance id.

The configuration exchange is independent of KIP-714 telemetry: a client may use one, the other or both, and they may go to different brokers. The plugins access the client instance id universally provided by KIP-1313. See detail of accessors below.

Configurations sent

A key is pushed when the cluster asks for it and the client is willing to send it. The cluster asks through the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys . The client decides whether to send the config or not based on three tiers:

TierDefinitionSent when
0. Never pushed
  • any key of type PASSWORD in Kafka's existing ConfigDef.Type
  • any key in the sasl., ssl. or security. families (as a prefix, or an infix such as producer.ssl.)
  • bootstrap.servers and bootstrap.controllers
  • never, even if requested
    • the client filters them out (no overrides)
    • exclusion hard-coded in every client implementation
1. Built-in
  • every other key defined in the client's own configuration definition (ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig, AdminClientConfig, StreamsConfig, ShareConsumerConfig), including Type.CLASS keys
  • the key is named in the requested set AND
  • not matched by config.push.denied.keys.
2. Custom
  • any key present in the client's configuration but not defined by the client (e.g., serializer/interceptor/partitioner/application settings, config.providers.*, and any other keys the application may add)
  • never in this KIP, even if named in the requested set
    • see Future Work for potential follow-ups


Other considerations:

  • requested keys the client does not define are ignored by the client
    • if a client sends one anyway, the broker drops it before invoking the plugin (see Broker Behavior).
  • requested keys are pushed whether or not they hold the default value, and a "Source" field added by this KIP to each entry (indicating if the value is default or user-defined).
  • tier 0 (never pushed) is filtered on the key, before any value is rendered, with the deny list supporting prefixes to easily reduce what is sent (e.g., any key in the form of sasl., ssl. or security.)
  • if nothing remains after filtering, the client sends nothing.
  • on every push the client logs at INFO the keys it pushed and the requested keys it filtered out, with the reason (tier 0, denied, not defined), never the values. With this an application can audit from its own log what left the process
  • custom keys are deferred. Keys the client does not define are the one category whose sensitivity Kafka cannot judge, and no requirement needs them yet. They are never pushed in this version, whatever the requested set says. The shape a later version would use, in which the application names the keys it is willing to share and the cluster opens the category, is recorded under Future Work.
  • class-name keys (key.serializer, value.deserializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes, partition.assignment.strategy, metric.reporters and similar) are tier 1:
    • when requested, the client pushes the fully qualified class names it is configured with, whether set by name or passed to the constructor;
    • they reveal the application's package naming and its choice of serializers, interceptors or partitioners, not credentials, endpoints or data, and they are among the most common root causes in client support cases;
    • none is in the default set, so they flow only when an operator requests them;
    • an application that prefers not to send them lists them in config.push.denied.keys, and an operator's plugin can drop them as well. Treating them as custom keys instead is listed under Rejected Alternatives.
    • Key names and tiers are the client library's own. The default requested set uses the Java client's names; a library whose names differ ignores names it does not define, and a library with a different naming convention adjusts its tier 0 rules accordingly
  • a few keys describe the environment rather than behavior: client.rack and, in Kafka Streams, application.server and state.dir. They are not sensitive configs filtered out by default, so an operator can request them by name; they are not in the default requested set, and an application that prefers not to send them can exclude them by adding them to config.push.denied.keys.

Default Configuration for Apache Kafka clients

The default value for the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys  is one list for all client types. It includes:

  • identity keys that let a plugin group snapshots by application, consumer group, transactional producer or Streams application (client.id, group.id, group.instance.id, transactional.id, application.id)
    • Note that these keys do not guarantee correlation between a restarted client and its predecessor,  as client instance id (KIP-1313) and the default client.id of a producer, consumer or admin client change at every start
  • client specific configs (all merged in a single list, defining the set of configs the broker/operator wants to "observe" from its clients, consumers, share consumers, producers and admins
  • the list contains no class names and no custom keys
  • each client sends the requested keys it supports and ignores the rest

Client Configuration Plugins

This KIP introduces a new broker-side interface named ClientConfigsPlugin.

  • invoked asynchronously with each accepted configuration snapshot
  • it does not validate the configuration
  • each implementation can take any desired action on the received config snapshot: log, forward it, store it, etc.
  • operators install an implementation through the broker configuration described later
  • no implementation shipped with Kafka
  • its shape follows the asynchronous plugin interface introduced by KIP-1331

End-to-end Flow [OUTDATED - WIP]

The following sequence diagram shows the flow between the various entities:

The flow includes the following steps:

  1. The client establishes a connection to the broker and sends an ApiVersions request
  2. If client.configs.plugin.class  is configured, the broker advertises GetClientConfigsSubscription  and PushClientConfigs  in the ApiVersions response
  3. From its network thread, the client sends a GetClientConfigsSubscription request to the least-loaded node that supports both RPCs
  4. GetClientConfigsSubscription response carries the keys the cluster requests
  5. If anything is requested, the client collects those keys under the tier rules, builds a PushClientConfigs request and sends it
  6. The broker validates the push (e.g., size), drops the entries the cluster did not request and any typed UNKNOWN, and calls ClientConfigsPlugin.onClientConfigs(), which returns a future
  7. The broker returns a successful PushClientConfigs  response without waiting for the future
  8. The client marks its exchange as complete for its lifetime. None of these steps blocks a user API call

Exceptions

The broker checks the serialized size of a push before invoking the plugin. If it exceeds client.configs.max.bytes, it returns CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE with the limit in the error message. Plugin failures are not reported to the client.

About rolls and restarts

  • enabling the feature is one broker roll (to set the plugin class) and no client restart. Every running client reconnects during the roll, sees the RPCs advertised for the first time, and runs its exchange.
  • a later change to the requested set is one command and no roll, but it reaches running clients only at their next restart (clients runs its exchange once at startup). Operators should adjust the list before enabling the plugin.
  • setting the list empty stops collection with the same command and no roll: clients that start afterwards receive nothing and send nothing

Protocol

GetClientConfigsSubscriptionRequest

The request has no specific fields in version 0: the client instance id arrives in the request header, selected through the headerVersions property that KIP-1313 adds to request schemas (header version 3 carries the client instance id).


GetClientConfigsSubscriptionResponse

Both RPCs are advertised only when client.configs.plugin.class is set on the broker.


PushClientConfigsRequest

Notes:

  • after a GetClientConfigsSubscription response that requests anything, the client sends the requested configs in one PushClientConfigsRequest, from its network thread and without blocking any user API call
  • the exchange runs once per client instance
  • the client retries only when no response arrives, using retry.backoff.ms within default.api.timeout.ms, and any response ends the exchange
  • Type is the ordinal of org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ConfigEntry.ConfigType. UNKNOWN means exactly one thing: the sending client does not define the key
    • such entries are not pushed in this version, and the broker drops any that arrive
    • a client library whose built-in type does not map onto ConfigEntry.ConfigType sends the key as STRING, never as UNKNOWN
  • Source tell where the config value comes from:
    • 0 for a default value
    • 1 for a value set by the application
    • 2 and above can be used future versions (e.g., 2 could be used for a broker-enforced value)
  • a Kafka Streams admin client sends two pushes of this RPC, one with ClientType=admin and one with ClientType=org.apache.kafka.streams (see Kafka Streams)


PushClientConfigsResponse

ErrorMessage carries a brief reason for an error (e.g., on CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE it states the broker's limit). This response does not wait for the plugin to run.

Errors

  • Both RPCs carry a top-level ErrorCode and ErrorMessage
  • Both RPCs can return UNSUPPORTED_VERSION if the feature is off on the broker (no plugin configured), or the requested version is not supported
  • PushClientConfigs can additionally return:
    • CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE:
      • indicates that the serialized snapshot exceeds the broker's client.configs.max.bytes
      • ErrorMessage states the limit
      • checked before the plugin is invoked
      • added by this KIP with its exception ClientConfigsTooLargeException, not retriable
    • INVALID_REQUEST:
      • malformed push (including a ClientType outside its format or length limit)
  • Client-side handling on any error:
    • log the broker's message once at WARN
    • end the exchange (no retry)
    • the client keeps operating normally and nothing reaches the application
    • only a missing response (timeout or disconnect) is retried, as described under Client Behavior
  • plugin outcomes are not reported to the client, so there is no plugin error code
  • throttling applies to both RPCs through ThrottleTimeMs and is not an error
  • pushing configurations is performed on a best-effort basis. Failure to send the configuration should not prevent the client from functioning.

Proposed Changes

Disabling the Feature

This feature can be disabled on the broker and the client.

For the broker, the feature is disabled by leaving the client.configs.plugin.class unset. The ApiVersions response then does not advertise the RPCs, and clients send nothing. With the plugin set but client.configs.requested.keys empty, clients ask once which keys are requested and nothing is collected. Given that this configuration is dynamic, this is a way of stopping collection without a broker roll.

For the client, set enable.config.push to false: the client does not send any of the 2 requests and behaves exactly like a client without the feature. 

Broker Behavior

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription and PushClientConfigs are included in ApiVersionsResponse only when client.configs.plugin.class is set
    • a request for either RPC while the feature is off gets a response with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
  • no authorization performed by the broker on any of the 2 RPCs
    • any authenticated client may ask what is requested and report its own configuration
    • the plugin receives the principal and may apply its own authorization rule
  • when receiving a GetClientConfigsSubscription request the broker just returns the current value of the config client.configs.requested.keys.The plugin is not invoked.
  • when receiving a PushClientConfigs request the broker performs the following steps in this order:
    • validate push
      • the broker validates the push, checking the serialized size of the configs against client.configs.max.bytes (CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE) and well-formedness, including the ClientType rule (INVALID_REQUEST), before anything else.
    • filter configs against the requested set
      • entries not named in the current requested set, and entries typed UNKNOWN (keys the sending client does not define), are dropped before the plugin and logged at DEBUG by key name. This makes the operator's setting hold for every client library, and "built-in keys only" hold even for a client that does not filter. If nothing remains, the push is acknowledged without invoking the plugin.
    • invoke plugin (returns a future)
    • respond with ErrorCode=NONE without waiting for the plugin's future
      • the future's outcome, including a synchronous throw, is recorded in the broker's metrics and logs and is not reported to the client
  • no storage or persisted state in the broker. Every accepted snapshot is handed to the plugin and then forgotten; a resend reaches the plugin again
    • with this, the broker cannot tell apart a client that is older than this KIP or has enable.config.push=false (sends neither request), a client that had nothing left after filtering (sends no push), a client whose push was rejected as too large, and a client that gave up after no response. Every request header carries the client instance id (KIP-1313), so a system that records instance ids can still list the instances that never pushed.

Configuration payload size enforcement

Clients only send the requested keys that belong to them, so a snapshot is small. As a backup, the broker checks the serialized size of every PushClientConfigs request against client.configs.max.bytes before invoking the plugin. If the request is larger, the broker answers CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE, with the limit in the error message, and nothing reaches the plugin.

A client's share of the default requested set is a few hundred bytes. The limit only matters if an operator requests every key a client defines. The table shows that worst case for the Java clients, so a default of 10 KB leaves room:

Excluding sensitive configurations

  • sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered (hardcoded sensitive set)
  • the broker does not check sensitivity
  • the broker only drops entries that are not in the requested set and entries typed UNKNOWN (see above)
  • a plugin may drop more (for example class-name keys); the client is not told about it
